label: Basic Concepts of Metric Geometry
notes: This opening chapter fixes the vocabulary that the whole book rests on. We move from a bare distance function to curves, their lengths, and the special distance-realizing paths called geodesics. Stress that everything here is metric-first: no smooth structure is assumed yet, only a distance obeying the triangle inequality.

label: Metric Spaces
notes: Recall the three axioms a metric must satisfy and contrast a genuine metric with a pseudometric, where distinct points may sit at distance zero. Emphasise that the triangle inequality is the single workhorse axiom: nearly every estimate later in the chapter is one application of it dressed in geometric language.

label: The Length of a Curve
notes: Define the length of a path as the supremum of polygonal approximations sampled along finer partitions. Point out that length always dominates the endpoint distance, and that a curve is rectifiable exactly when this supremum is finite. The gap between length and distance is what later measures inefficiency of a path.

label: Geodesics as Isometric Embeddings
notes: A geodesic is an isometric embedding of a real interval: distance along the image equals distance in the parameter. Stress that this is a global, length-realizing condition, far stronger than the differential-geometry notion. Linear reparametrisation by arc length is the convention, so speed is constant and equal to one.

label: Segments, Rays, and Lines
notes: Classify geodesics by the domain interval: a compact interval gives a segment joining two points, a half-line gives a ray, and the whole real line gives a bi-infinite geodesic line. Each is an isometric image, so the three differ only in how far the distance-realizing path is allowed to extend.

label: Geodesic Spaces
notes: A space is geodesic when every pair of points is joined by at least one geodesic segment. Note this is genuinely an existence hypothesis: a punctured plane or an open disc fails it. The Hopf-Rinow theorem, met later, gives the standard sufficient conditions of completeness and local compactness.

label: Uniquely Geodesic Spaces
notes: Uniqueness is separate from existence. The sphere is geodesic yet antipodal points are joined by infinitely many great-circle arcs. Non-positive curvature, the theme of the book, will force uniqueness. Use the antipodal picture to make vivid that branching of geodesics is exactly the failure curvature controls.

label: Geodesic vs Non-Geodesic Paths
notes: Contrast a straight distance-realizing segment with a wandering curve sharing the same endpoints. The wandering curve has strictly greater length while the segment achieves the infimum. This picture is the intuitive core of the word geodesic: it is the path that spends no length on detours between its endpoints.

label: Metric versus Induced Length Metric
notes: Given any metric one can define the induced length metric by infimising path length between points. The two agree in geodesic spaces but can differ sharply otherwise. The classic example is two points on a circle in the plane: the chord distance versus the arc distance you must travel within the curve.

label: Local Geodesics
notes: A local geodesic realizes distance only on short subintervals, not globally. On a flat cylinder a helix winding around is locally geodesic but not globally minimizing. Emphasise that every geodesic is local but the converse fails, and that this gap is where interesting global geometry lives.

label: Convex Subsets and Functions
notes: A subset is convex when it contains a geodesic between any two of its points, and a function is convex when its restriction to every geodesic is convex in the ordinary sense. Convexity of the distance function will be the analytic signature of non-positive curvature throughout the book.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: Recap the chain: metric, then curve length, then geodesic as isometric embedding, then existence and uniqueness, then convexity. Each link is checkable on small finite examples. Preview that comparison triangles and Alexandrov angles in the next sections turn these qualitative pictures into curvature inequalities.
